apmo-2026-01.title: Assume $a\ge p$ and work modulo small prime powers
apmo-2026-01.body:
By symmetry assume $a\ge p$. Recall that a perfect power $m^o$ with $o\ge2$ is never $\equiv2\pmod4$ (if $m$ is even it is $\equiv0$, if $m$ is odd it is odd).

**$p\ge4$ is impossible.** Then $4\mid a!$ and $4\mid p!$, so $m^o=a!+p!-26\equiv-26\equiv2\pmod 4$, a contradiction.

**Case $p=1$:** $a!=m^o+25\ge26$, so $a\ge5$. Then $a!$ is even and divisible by $5$, so $m^o=a!-25$ is odd and divisible by $5$: $m$ is odd and $5\mid m$. If $o$ were even, $m^o$ would be an odd square, $\equiv1\pmod4$, giving $a!\equiv26\equiv2\pmod 4$, impossible. So $o\ge3$ and $125\mid m^o$, hence $a!\equiv25\pmod{125}$. Then $v_5(a!)=2$ exactly, which means $10\le a\le14$. Write $a!=25u$ with $5\nmid u$; we need $125\mid 25(u-1)$, i.e. $u\equiv1\pmod5$. Modulo $5$: $10!/25=145152\equiv2$, and multiplying successively by $11,12,13,14\equiv1,2,3,4$ gives $u\equiv2,4,2,3$ for $a=11,12,13,14$. None is $\equiv1$, so there is no solution.

**Case $p=2$:** $a!=m^o+24\ge25$, so $a\ge5$. If $a=5$, $m^o=96=2^5\cdot3$, which is not a perfect power with exponent $\ge2$ (the prime $3$ appears only once). If $a\ge6$, then $9\mid a!$, so $m^o\equiv-24\equiv3\pmod 9$. Hence $3\mid m$, but then $9\mid m^o$, a contradiction.

**Case $p=3$:** $a!=m^o+20\ge21$, so $a\ge4$.
- $a=4$: $m^o=4=2^2$, so $(m,o)=(2,2)$.
- $a=5$: $m^o=100=2^2\cdot5^2$, so $o\mid2$ and $(m,o)=(10,2)$.
- $a\ge6$: $16\mid a!$, so $m^o\equiv-20\equiv12\pmod{16}$. Thus $v_2(m^o)=o\,v_2(m)=2$, forcing $o=2$ and $m=2k$ with $k$ odd. Then $m^2=4k^2\equiv4\pmod{32}$ (since $k^2\equiv1\pmod8$), so $m^2\equiv4\not\equiv12\pmod{16}$, a contradiction.

**Check:** $4!+3!=30=2^2+26$ and $5!+3!=126=10^2+26$. Adding the symmetric solutions:

**Answer:** $(a,p,m,o)\in\{(4,3,2,2),\,(3,4,2,2),\,(5,3,10,2),\,(3,5,10,2)\}$. ∎

apmo-2026-02.title: Count "both in" and "both out" for each element
apmo-2026-02.body:
Let $X$ be the $n$-element set, take indices modulo $N=2^n$ (so $A_{N+1}=A_1$), and let $T=\sum_{i=1}^{N}|A_i\cap A_{i+1}|$ be the sum in question. Write $\overline Y=X\setminus Y$.

**Step 1: "both in" equals "both out".** Fix $x\in X$ and go once around the cycle $A_1,A_2,\dots,A_N,A_1$. Let $n_{11},n_{10},n_{01},n_{00}$ be the numbers of indices $i$ for which ($x\in A_i$?, $x\in A_{i+1}$?) is (yes, yes), (yes, no), (no, yes), (no, no). Exactly half of all subsets contain $x$, so $2^{n-1}$ indices $i$ have $x\in A_i$, and also $2^{n-1}$ indices have $x\in A_{i+1}$:
$$n_{11}+n_{10}=2^{n-1}=n_{11}+n_{01},\qquad n_{00}+n_{01}=2^{n-1}.$$
The first gives $n_{10}=n_{01}$, and then $n_{00}=2^{n-1}-n_{01}=2^{n-1}-n_{10}=n_{11}$.

Summing $n_{11}$ over all $x$ gives $T$, and summing $n_{00}$ gives $\sum_i|\overline{A_i}\cap\overline{A_{i+1}}|$. Therefore
$$T=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}t_i,\qquad t_i=|A_i\cap A_{i+1}|+|\overline{A_i\cup A_{i+1}}| .$$

**Step 2: no two consecutive $t_i$ vanish.** $t_i=0$ means $A_i\cap A_{i+1}=\varnothing$ and $A_i\cup A_{i+1}=X$, i.e. $A_{i+1}=\overline{A_i}$. If $t_i=t_{i+1}=0$ then $A_{i+2}=\overline{A_{i+1}}=A_i$; but $N\ge4$, so $i+2\not\equiv i\pmod N$, and the sets are distinct, a contradiction.

**Step 3.** Since $N$ is even, group the terms into the $N/2$ pairs $(t_1,t_2),(t_3,t_4),\dots,(t_{N-1},t_N)$. Each pair consists of non-negative integers that are not both $0$, so has sum $\ge1$. Hence $\sum t_i\ge N/2=2^{n-1}$ and
$$T\ge\frac{2^{n-1}}2=2^{n-2}.\qquad ∎$$

apmo-2026-03.title: Injectivity, midpoints, then dyadic density
apmo-2026-03.body:
**These work.** If $f(x)=ax+b$ with $a\ne0$, then $|f(u)-f(w)|=|a|\,|u-w|$ for all $u,w$, so the two inequalities are equivalent.

**No others.** Let $f$ satisfy the condition $(\star)$.

*Equal distances.* Exchanging $x$ and $z$ in $(\star)$ gives: $|z-y|<|y-x|$ iff $|f(z)-f(y)|<|f(y)-f(x)|$. So if $|x-y|=|y-z|$, neither $f$-inequality is strict:
$$|x-y|=|y-z|\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x)-f(y)|=|f(y)-f(z)|. \tag{1}$$

*Injectivity.* If $f(y)=f(z)$ with $y\ne z$, take $x=y$: then $|x-y|=0<|y-z|$, so $(\star)$ gives $0=|f(x)-f(y)|<|f(y)-f(z)|=0$, impossible.

*Midpoints.* Let $x\ne z$ and $y=\frac{x+z}2$. By (1), $f(y)-f(x)=\pm\bigl(f(z)-f(y)\bigr)$. The minus sign would give $f(x)=f(z)$, contradicting injectivity. Hence
$$f\Big(\frac{x+z}2\Big)=\frac{f(x)+f(z)}2\qquad\text{for all }x,z>0. \tag{2}$$

*Normalise.* If $f$ satisfies $(\star)$, so does $af+b$ for constants $a\ne0$, $b$. Since $f(1)\ne f(2)$, the function $g(x)=1+\dfrac{f(x)-f(1)}{f(2)-f(1)}$ satisfies $(\star)$ and (2), with $g(1)=1$, $g(2)=2$. We show $g(x)=x$ for all $x$; then $f$ is of the form $ax+b$.

*Dyadic rationals.* By (2) with $x=k-1$, $z=k+1$: $g(k+1)=2g(k)-g(k-1)$ for $k\ge2$, so by induction $g(k)=k$ for all positive integers $k$. Suppose $g(m/2^j)=m/2^j$ for all positive integers $m$ (true for $j=0$). For $j+1$: if $m$ is even this is the hypothesis; if $m\ge3$ is odd, $\frac m{2^{j+1}}$ is the midpoint of $\frac{m-1}{2^{j+1}}$ and $\frac{m+1}{2^{j+1}}$ (even numerators, positive), so (2) gives $g(\frac m{2^{j+1}})=\frac m{2^{j+1}}$; finally $\frac2{2^{j+1}}$ is the midpoint of $\frac1{2^{j+1}}$ and $\frac3{2^{j+1}}$, so $g(\frac1{2^{j+1}})=2\cdot\frac1{2^j}-\frac3{2^{j+1}}=\frac1{2^{j+1}}$. Thus $g(q)=q$ for every positive dyadic rational $q$.

*All reals.* Fix $x>0$ and a positive dyadic $y$. For every positive dyadic $d$, put $z=y+d$ (also a positive dyadic). Then $g(y)=y$, $g(z)=z$, and $(\star)$ says
$$|x-y|<d\iff|g(x)-y|<d .$$
If $|x-y|<|g(x)-y|$, a dyadic $d$ strictly between them violates this; similarly in the other case. Hence $|g(x)-y|=|x-y|$, i.e. $g(x)\in\{x,\,2y-x\}$, for **every** positive dyadic $y$. If $g(x)\ne x$, then $g(x)=2y-x$ for two different dyadics $y$, which is impossible. So $g(x)=x$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=ax+b$ for real constants $a\ne0$ and $b$. ∎

apmo-2026-04.title: Common tangency point, two homotheties, and coordinates
apmo-2026-04.body:
Let $r$ be the radius of $\omega$, let $r_1$ and $J$ be the inradius and incentre of triangle $ABD$, and $r_2$, $K$ those of triangle $CBD$. The quadrilateral is convex (it has an incircle), so $A$ and $C$ lie on opposite sides of $BD$ and $E$ lies on both diagonals.

**Step 1: both incircles touch $BD$ at the same point $S$.** By tangent lengths, the incircle of $ABD$ touches $BD$ at the point $S$ with $BS=\frac{AB+BD-AD}2$, and the incircle of $CBD$ touches it at $S'$ with $BS'=\frac{CB+BD-CD}2$. Since $ABCD$ has an incircle, $AB+CD=BC+DA$, i.e. $AB-AD=CB-CD$, so $S=S'$.

**Coordinates.** Take $S$ as origin and $BD$ as the $x$-axis, with $A$ in the upper half-plane. Then $J=(0,r_1)$ and $K=(0,-r_2)$. Let $I=(u,v)$, and let
$$P'=(u,\,v+r),\qquad Q=(u,\,v-r)$$
be the endpoints of the diameter of $\omega$ perpendicular to $BD$ (the top and bottom points of $\omega$). We will show that $P'$ lies on ray $EJ$ beyond $J$; since $P'I\perp BD$, this is the required statement.

**Step 2: $r>r_1$ and $r>r_2$, and the positions of $A$, $C$.** The circle $\omega$ and the incircle of $ABD$ are both tangent to the two sides of angle $BAD$ (inside it), so the homothety $h$ with centre $A$ and ratio $k=r/r_1>0$ maps the incircle of $ABD$ onto $\omega$. It preserves directions, so it maps the bottom point $S$ of the small circle to the bottom point $Q$ of $\omega$: $Q-A=k(S-A)$, i.e. $Q=(1-k)A$. Now $\omega$ touches side $BC$ at an interior point of that side, which lies strictly below $BD$; hence $Q$ is strictly below $BD$, and since $A$ is above, $1-k<0$, i.e. $r>r_1$. Thus
$$A=-\alpha Q,\qquad \alpha=\frac{r_1}{r-r_1}>0 .$$
In the same way the homothety with centre $C$ and ratio $r/r_2$ maps the incircle of $CBD$ (top point $S$) onto $\omega$ (top point $P'$), $r>r_2$, and
$$C=-\gamma P',\qquad \gamma=\frac{r_2}{r-r_2}>0 .$$

**Step 3: $(r+v):(r-v)=r_1:r_2$.** Let $\angle ABD=2\beta_1$ and $\angle DBC=2\beta_2$, and $t=BS>0$. Since $J$ is on the bisector of $\angle ABD$ and $S$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $J$, $r_1=t\tan\beta_1$; similarly $r_2=t\tan\beta_2$ (same point $S$, by Step 1). The ray $BD$ lies inside angle $ABC=2\beta_1+2\beta_2$, and $I$ lies on its bisector at distance $\rho=BI$ from $B$. Measuring angles from ray $BD$ towards $A$, ray $BA$ is at angle $2\beta_1$, ray $BC$ at $-2\beta_2$, so ray $BI$ is at angle $\beta_1-\beta_2$. Hence the signed height of $I$ and its distance to $BA$ are
$$v=\rho\sin(\beta_1-\beta_2),\qquad r=\rho\sin(\beta_1+\beta_2).$$
Therefore $r+v=2\rho\sin\beta_1\cos\beta_2$ and $r-v=2\rho\cos\beta_1\sin\beta_2$, so
$$\frac{r+v}{r-v}=\frac{\tan\beta_1}{\tan\beta_2}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}.$$
As $(r+v)+(r-v)=2r$, this gives $r+v=\mu r_1$ and $r-v=\mu r_2$ with $\mu=\dfrac{2r}{r_1+r_2}>1$ (by Step 2). So
$$P'=(u,\mu r_1),\quad Q=(u,-\mu r_2),\quad A=(-\alpha u,\ \alpha\mu r_2),\quad C=(-\gamma u,\ -\gamma\mu r_1).$$

**Step 4: compute $E$.** $A$ is above and $C$ below the $x$-axis, and the point of segment $AC$ on the $x$-axis is
$$E=\frac{y_A\,C-y_C\,A}{y_A-y_C},\qquad x_E=\frac{\alpha\mu r_2(-\gamma u)-\gamma\mu r_1\,\alpha u}{\alpha\mu r_2+\gamma\mu r_1}=-\frac{\alpha\gamma\,(r_1+r_2)}{\alpha r_2+\gamma r_1}\,u .$$
Now $\alpha r_2+\gamma r_1=r_1r_2\Big(\dfrac1{r-r_1}+\dfrac1{r-r_2}\Big)=\dfrac{r_1r_2\,(2r-r_1-r_2)}{(r-r_1)(r-r_2)}$ and $\alpha\gamma=\dfrac{r_1r_2}{(r-r_1)(r-r_2)}$, so
$$x_E=-\frac{(r_1+r_2)\,u}{2r-r_1-r_2}=-\frac{u}{\mu-1},\qquad E=\Big(-\frac{u}{\mu-1},\,0\Big).$$

**Step 5: conclusion.** The point $E+\mu(J-E)$ has coordinates
$$\Big(x_E(1-\mu),\ \mu r_1\Big)=(u,\ \mu r_1)=P'.$$
Since $\mu>1$, $P'$ lies on ray $EJ$ beyond $J$. So the extension of ray $EJ$ meets $\omega$ at $P=P'$, and $PI$ is the diameter of $\omega$ perpendicular to $BD$. Hence $PI\perp BD$. ∎

apmo-2026-05.title: Doors inside the end rows are irrelevant; duality halves the rest
apmo-2026-05.body:
Call a choice of locked doors *good* if some room of row $1$ is joined to some room of row $n+1$ through unlocked doors. Write room $(r,j)$ for row $r\in\{1,\dots,n+1\}$, column $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. There are $n\cdot n$ doors between consecutive rows and $(n+1)(n-1)$ doors inside rows, $2n^2-1$ in total.

**Step 1: doors inside row $1$ and row $n+1$ do not matter.** If a walk through unlocked doors goes from row $1$ to row $n+1$, take the part from its last visit to row $1$ before its first visit to row $n+1$, up to that first visit. This part uses no door inside row $1$ or row $n+1$. So goodness depends only on the other $M=n^2+(n-1)^2=2n^2-2n+1$ doors, the *relevant* ones, and the answer is $2^{2n-2}$ times the number of good configurations of the relevant doors. We show that exactly half of the $2^M$ configurations are good.

**Step 2: the wall graph.** Draw the grid as the rectangle $[0,n]\times[0,n+1]$, with room $(r,j)$ the unit square $[j-1,j]\times[n+1-r,\,n+2-r]$. Each door is the unit segment (wall) shared by its two rooms. The relevant walls are the horizontal segments on the lines $y=h$, $1\le h\le n$, and the vertical segments on the lines $x=1,\dots,n-1$ between heights $1$ and $n$. Let $\mathcal W$ be the graph whose vertices are the lattice points $(x,h)$ with $1\le x\le n-1$, $1\le h\le n$, together with a vertex $L$ (the left side $x=0$) and a vertex $R$ (the right side $x=n$). Its edges are the relevant walls, joining their endpoints, with an endpoint on $x=0$ read as $L$ and one on $x=n$ read as $R$. A wall is *closed* if its door is locked.

**Key claim.** A configuration is good $\iff$ there is **no** path from $L$ to $R$ in $\mathcal W$ made of closed walls.

*($\Leftarrow$)* Suppose the configuration is not good. Let $U$ be the set of rooms reachable from row $1$ through unlocked relevant doors, together with all of row $1$; no room of row $n+1$ is in $U$. Let $\mathcal B$ be the set of walls separating a room of $U$ from a room not in $U$. Every such door is locked (otherwise the outside room would be in $U$), so the walls in $\mathcal B$ are closed. Also $\mathcal B$ contains only relevant walls, because walls inside row $1$ or row $n+1$ separate two rooms on the same side. Consider the degrees in the graph $(\mathcal W,\mathcal B)$:
- At an interior lattice point, the walls meeting there separate cyclically consecutive squares among the four squares around the point. Going once around, membership in $U$ changes an even number of times, so the degree is even.
- The edges at $L$ are the walls between $(r,1)$ and $(r+1,1)$. Going down column $1$ from row $1$ (in $U$) to row $n+1$ (not in $U$), membership changes an odd number of times, so $\deg L$ is odd. Likewise $\deg R$ is odd.

In the connected component of $L$ the number of odd-degree vertices is even (handshake lemma), so $R$ is in this component. This gives a path of closed walls from $L$ to $R$.

*($\Rightarrow$)* Suppose there is a path from $L$ to $R$ of closed walls. Then there is also a simple one, $\pi$. For a room $\rho$ in column $j$, let $\sigma(\rho)$ be the parity of the number of horizontal walls of $\pi$ in column $j$ lying below $\rho$ (at heights $h\le$ the bottom height of $\rho$).
- For vertically adjacent rooms, $\sigma$ differs exactly when the wall between them belongs to $\pi$.
- For horizontally adjacent rooms $(r,j),(r,j+1)$ with $2\le r\le n$, let $h_0=n+1-r$ and add up the $\pi$-degrees of the points $(j,1),\dots,(j,h_0)$. Each is $0$ or $2$, because the ends of $\pi$ are $L$ and $R$. The sum counts the horizontal $\pi$-walls of columns $j$ and $j+1$ at heights $\le h_0$, every vertical $\pi$-wall between two of these points twice, and the wall from $(j,h_0)$ to $(j,h_0+1)$, which separates our two rooms, once. Hence $\sigma(r,j)\ne\sigma(r,j+1)$ exactly when that wall is in $\pi$. The same count with $h_0=n$ shows that all rooms of row $1$ have the same $\sigma$, because $\mathcal W$ has no vertical walls above height $n$.
- Rooms of row $n+1$ have nothing below them: $\sigma=0$. In column $1$ every horizontal wall ends at $L$, and the simple path $\pi$ uses exactly one edge at $L$, so $\sigma(1,1)=1$. Hence $\sigma=1$ on all of row $1$.

Passing through an unlocked door never changes $\sigma$: the door's wall is not closed, so it is not in $\pi$, and inside rows $1$ and $n+1$, $\sigma$ is constant anyway. So no walk through unlocked doors leads from row $1$ ($\sigma=1$) to row $n+1$ ($\sigma=0$), and the configuration is not good.

**Step 3: rotate.** Let $\mathcal G$ be the graph of relevant doors: vertices are a vertex $A$ (row $1$), a vertex $B$ (row $n+1$) and the rooms of rows $2,\dots,n$, and edges are the relevant doors. The map $(x,h)\mapsto$ room $(x+1,h)$, $L\mapsto A$, $R\mapsto B$, is an isomorphism $\varphi:\mathcal W\to\mathcal G$. It sends the horizontal walls at height $h$ (a path $L,(1,h),\dots,(n-1,h),R$) to the doors of column $h$ (the path $A,(2,h),\dots,(n,h),B$), and the vertical wall $(x,h)$–$(x,h+1)$ to the door between $(x+1,h)$ and $(x+1,h+1)$. For a configuration $H$, define $H^*$ by declaring the door $\varphi(w)$ **unlocked** in $H^*$ exactly when the wall $w$ is closed in $H$. This is a bijection on configurations (complement, then relabel). Moreover
$$H^*\text{ good}\iff\text{closed walls of }H\text{ join }L\text{ to }R\iff H\text{ not good},$$
by the key claim. So $H\mapsto H^*$ maps good configurations injectively into bad ones and bad ones injectively into good ones. Hence exactly half, $2^{M-1}=2^{2n^2-2n}$, of the configurations of relevant doors are good.

**Answer:** $2^{2n^2-2n}\cdot2^{2n-2}=2^{2n^2-2}$ (checked by brute force for $n=1,2,3$: $1,\,64,\,65536$). ∎
